quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Countries that export a wide range of sophisticated products tend to grow faster than those that rely on a few raw materials. Economists describe this by saying that a country's export basket reveals the accumulated know-how of its workers and firms. Moving into a new product is easier when it draws on skills that already exist, which is why a car maker can shift to making aircraft parts more readily than a coffee grower can. This suggests that development follows paths shaped by what a country already does. Critics warn that such analysis may discourage risky leaps that have sometimes paid off, as in economies that built entire industries from little. Supporters reply that leaps succeed mainly when they build on hidden capabilities. Policymakers are therefore advised to look for neighbouring products rather than distant ones. Yet no formula can identify which neighbours will prove profitable. Strategy must combine analysis with experimentation.
options: Development follows paths shaped by existing know-how and analysis of neighbouring products cannot replace experimentation.
Critics argue that development paths are fixed by existing skills, so risky leaps cannot succeed.
A car maker can shift to aircraft parts because economists have shown that leaps succeed without capabilities.
Countries grow faster when they export raw materials, since simple products require little accumulated know-how.
quests.correctAnswer: Development follows paths shaped by existing know-how and analysis of neighbouring products cannot replace experimentation.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that says what analysis can and cannot deliver, then see which option honours both halves.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains why development is path-dependent, considers the objection about leaps and ends by limiting what analysis can promise. The wrong options reverse the growth pattern, turn an example into a universal claim and misstate the critics.
keyPoints: Diverse, sophisticated exports are linked to faster growth.
New products are easier to enter when they use existing skills.
Analysis of neighbouring products guides policy but must be combined with experimentation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Legal documents are often written in a dense style that ordinary readers struggle to follow. Plain-language reformers argue that contracts, statutes and court notices should be redrafted so that people can understand their rights and duties. Trials of simplified forms have shown that recipients respond more accurately and more quickly. Some lawyers object that legal terms have settled meanings built up by centuries of court decisions, so replacing them with everyday words may create uncertainty. Reformers answer that the risk is small when new drafts are tested carefully. There is also a question of professional interest, since complexity keeps intermediaries in demand. Several governments have adopted plain-language standards for official notices while leaving specialist contracts largely untouched. This division reflects a pragmatic judgement about where clarity matters most. The debate is really about who a legal text is for.
options: Lawyers support plain language because legal terms lack settled meaning built by centuries of decisions.
Reformers argue that specialist contracts should be simplified first, since intermediaries benefit from complexity there.
Simplified forms confuse recipients, which is why governments have kept official notices in traditional legal language.
Plain-language legal reform helps ordinary readers, but fears about precision mean governments apply it selectively.
quests.correctAnswer: Plain-language legal reform helps ordinary readers, but fears about precision mean governments apply it selectively.
quests.hint: Notice what the paragraph says about where governments have actually applied the reform.
quests.explanation: Trials show benefits for readers, lawyers raise precision concerns and governments choose to simplify official notices first, which shows a pragmatic compromise. The wrong options reverse trial results, lawyers' position and the order of reform.
keyPoints: Dense legal writing is hard for ordinary readers to follow.
Simplified forms improve responses, but lawyers fear losing settled meaning.
Governments simplify official notices while leaving specialist contracts largely untouched.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Scientific knowledge is a public good: once a discovery is published, anyone can use it without reducing the supply available to others. Markets tend to underprovide such goods, since those who pay for research cannot capture all the benefits. Governments therefore fund a large share of basic science, and universities and charities contribute as well. Yet public funding creates its own difficulties, because officials must choose among projects whose value is uncertain by nature. Peer review helps, but it favours ideas that resemble those already accepted. Some funders set aside money for high-risk proposals, accepting that most will fail. Others experiment with prizes that reward results rather than promises. A striking feature of the record is how often major advances came from work that seemed useless at the time. That history argues for patience, but it does not tell any single committee which uncertain project to back.
options: Major advances usually came from work that seemed valuable at the time, so committees can identify winners.
Public funding supports basic science and choosing which uncertain projects to back remains inherently difficult and contested.
Peer review favours unconventional ideas, so high-risk proposals seldom need separate funding.
Markets provide scientific knowledge efficiently, so governments fund basic science to reduce private costs.
quests.correctAnswer: Public funding supports basic science and choosing which uncertain projects to back remains inherently difficult and contested.
quests.hint: Decide whether the paragraph ends with a solution or with a persistent difficulty.
quests.explanation: The economic logic explains public funding, and the rest shows the difficulty of choosing among unknowable projects, which history illustrates without resolving. The wrong options reverse market provision, peer review's bias and the history of discoveries.
keyPoints: Published science is a public good, so markets underprovide it.
Governments fund basic research, but must choose among uncertain projects.
History shows valuable advances from apparently useless work, which does not identify which projects to back.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Dense cities can bring people into contact with more neighbours, shops and public spaces, and some researchers argue that this encourages trust. Others find that trust is higher in small towns, where people are likely to meet the same faces repeatedly. Studies that control for income and age suggest that neither density nor size has a consistent effect. What appears to matter more is the presence of shared places where different groups meet without pressure, such as libraries, parks and markets. When such spaces are absent or unsafe, people retreat into private life, however close their neighbours are. Planners can influence this by designing streets for lingering rather than for speed alone. Even so, trust also depends on factors outside urban design, including inequality and local history. A city's form provides opportunities for contact, but people must choose to use them.
options: Trust is unaffected by shared places, because studies show inequality is the main factor in social trust.
Social trust depends less on density than on shared public places and wider conditions such as inequality and local history.
Dense cities produce more trust than small towns, since residents there meet a wider variety of people.
Streets designed for lingering guarantee that neighbours will use public spaces and trust each other.
quests.correctAnswer: Social trust depends less on density than on shared public places and wider conditions such as inequality and local history.
quests.hint: Compare what the paragraph rules out with what it says matters more.
quests.explanation: Density alone does not explain trust, shared places matter, and wider factors also limit what design can achieve. The wrong options revive density as the cause, deny the role of places and overstate design.
keyPoints: Neither city density nor town size consistently explains social trust.
Shared, safe places where groups meet appear to matter more.
Design offers opportunities, but inequality and history also shape trust.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: After the plague of the fourteenth century killed a large share of Europe's population, labour became scarce. Surviving workers could demand higher wages and better conditions, and some rulers responded with laws that tried to freeze pay at former levels. These laws were widely evaded, because employers competed for workers. In regions where landlords held strong legal power over peasants, however, lords could tighten control, and serfdom lasted longer. Historians therefore argue that the same demographic shock produced different outcomes depending on institutions. Where peasants could leave and negotiate, wages rose and the old bonds weakened. Where they could not, the shortage increased the pressure to bind them. The episode is often cited to show that economic forces shape society, but the evidence shows that political arrangements decide which way those forces push. Crisis creates openings, and institutions determine who benefits.
options: Wage-freezing laws succeeded in most regions, because employers cooperated to keep pay at former levels.
Historians say that economic forces alone decided outcomes, so political arrangements made little difference.
Serfdom weakened after the plague, since labour shortages favour workers over landlords.
The plague's labour shortage had different outcomes because institutions decided whether workers or landlords benefited.
quests.correctAnswer: The plague's labour shortage had different outcomes because institutions decided whether workers or landlords benefited.
quests.hint: Locate the claim about what decides the direction of economic forces.
quests.explanation: The paragraph uses one shock to show that institutions mediate its effects, so results differed. The wrong options reverse the fate of wage laws, overgeneralise the effect on serfdom and dismiss institutions.
keyPoints: The fourteenth-century plague made labour scarce in Europe.
Where peasants could leave and bargain, wages rose; where landlords were strong, control tightened.
Political institutions shaped how the shock played out.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Interoperability, the ability of different services to exchange messages and data, is often proposed as a way to reduce the power of large platforms. If users of a small network could message friends on a larger one, they would no longer be forced to join the biggest network simply because their friends are there. This could lower the barrier for new competitors. However, interoperability raises technical and social difficulties. Different services enforce different rules on privacy, security and moderation, and connecting them may expose users to the weakest standard among them. Platforms also worry that openness will let rivals benefit from their investment. Some regulators have introduced requirements limited to basic messaging, watching the effects before going further. Whether interoperability will encourage competition or merely spread problems across networks is not yet known. The answer will depend on how the technical details are set.
options: Interoperability could weaken platform lock-in and risks and unknown effects make regulators cautious.
Interoperability guarantees more competition because users can leave a large network without losing their contacts.
Regulators have already required full interoperability across services, having proved its benefits for competition.
Platforms welcome openness because rivals cannot benefit from their investment when services exchange messages.
quests.correctAnswer: Interoperability could weaken platform lock-in and risks and unknown effects make regulators cautious.
quests.hint: See which option treats the outcome as still open, as the paragraph does near its end.
quests.explanation: The idea attacks a real barrier but brings risks and uncertainties, so regulators start with limited requirements. The wrong options claim a guaranteed effect, reverse platforms' concerns and treat a trial as a full mandate.
keyPoints: Interoperability would let users of small networks reach friends on large ones.
It could lower barriers to competitors but may expose users to weaker standards.
Regulators start with basic messaging, and the results are not yet known.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Eyewitness memory is far less reliable than juries tend to assume. People reconstruct events each time they recall them, and details can be altered by questions, by conversations with other witnesses or by exposure to news reports. Confidence, moreover, is a poor guide to accuracy: a witness may be entirely sure and still wrong. Research has shown that identification procedures, such as showing suspects one at a time and recording the witness's confidence immediately, can reduce mistaken identifications. Some courts now warn juries about the limits of memory, while others allow psychologists to testify. Reform has been slow because vivid testimony feels convincing, and because police and prosecutors may not welcome methods that lower the number of identifications. Innocent people have been convicted on the strength of confident but mistaken witnesses. Better procedures cannot repair memory, but they can protect it from contamination.
options: Better procedures repair memory itself, so juries do not need warnings about the limits of recall.
Witnesses who feel confident are usually accurate, so identification procedures need little reform.
Reform has been rapid because police and prosecutors welcome methods that reduce identifications.
Eyewitness memory is malleable and confidence misleading, so procedures can limit but not remove error.
quests.correctAnswer: Eyewitness memory is malleable and confidence misleading, so procedures can limit but not remove error.
quests.hint: Read the last sentence for what better procedures can and cannot do.
quests.explanation: Memory is reconstructive and confidence misleading, and procedures reduce contamination but cannot restore accuracy. The wrong options reverse the link between confidence and accuracy, the pace of reform and the effect of procedures.
keyPoints: People reconstruct memories each time, and confidence does not guarantee accuracy.
Sequential lineups and recorded confidence reduce mistaken identifications.
Reform has been slow, and procedures protect memory but cannot repair it.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Historians of protest have found that nonviolent campaigns have succeeded more often than violent ones in achieving their goals over the past century. Explanations include the fact that nonviolence can draw in large numbers of participants, including those who would not risk injury. Broad participation makes it harder for authorities to portray a movement as extremist, and it increases the chance that some officials or soldiers will refuse to act against it. Critics point out that the comparison may be affected by the kinds of goals chosen and by the regimes involved. Nonviolent campaigns have failed too, especially against governments willing to use extreme repression and to control information. Some scholars add that the two approaches are seldom pure, since threats of disruption often accompany peaceful demonstrations. The pattern is a tendency, not a law. What seems consistent is that success depends on winning support rather than on the tactic in itself.
options: Nonviolent campaigns have tended to succeed by mobilising broad support and context and repression matter.
Scholars say the two approaches are separate, so peaceful protests seldom involve threats of disruption.
Nonviolent campaigns succeed against repressive governments, since broad participation prevents the use of force.
Violent campaigns attract more participants, which explains why historians find them more successful.
quests.correctAnswer: Nonviolent campaigns have tended to succeed by mobilising broad support and context and repression matter.
quests.hint: Notice which words mark the finding as a tendency rather than a rule.
quests.explanation: The paragraph reports a pattern, explains it through participation and defections, then qualifies it with counterexamples and confounding factors. The wrong options turn a tendency into a guarantee, reverse who attracts participants and deny mixed tactics.
keyPoints: Nonviolent campaigns have more often achieved their goals than violent ones.
They attract broad participation and may prompt defections, though critics note confounding factors.
Repression can defeat them, and success depends on winning support.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some countries now require large companies to check their supply chains for abuses such as forced labour and to report what they find. Supporters say that firms profit from cheap goods and should therefore take responsibility for how they are made. Companies reply that supply chains stretch across many countries and layers of subcontractors, so complete visibility is impossible. Auditing itself has weaknesses, since factories can hide problems during announced visits and workers may fear speaking honestly. Some firms have responded by shortening their supply chains or by shifting orders away from risky regions, which can leave the workers there without income. Advocates argue that requiring companies to work with suppliers to improve conditions, rather than simply drop them, is more constructive. Legal penalties encourage effort but can also encourage box-ticking. Meaningful change probably depends on long-term relationships and on the involvement of workers themselves.
options: Complete visibility of supply chains is straightforward for companies, so due-diligence laws impose little burden.
Announced audits reliably expose abuses, because workers speak honestly when visits are planned in advance.
Due-diligence laws push companies to address abuses, but lasting change needs partnerships and worker involvement.
Withdrawing orders from risky regions protects workers there, so advocates recommend it over improving conditions.
quests.correctAnswer: Due-diligence laws push companies to address abuses, but lasting change needs partnerships and worker involvement.
quests.hint: Find the position the advocates take on how companies should respond to problems.
quests.explanation: The laws seek accountability, yet auditing is imperfect and exit can hurt workers, so the paragraph concludes that partnership and worker voice matter. The wrong options reverse visibility, audit reliability and the effect of withdrawal.
keyPoints: Some laws require companies to check supply chains for abuses.
Complete visibility is hard, audits have weaknesses, and dropping suppliers can harm workers.
Long-term relationships and worker involvement are needed for real change.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Modern medicine has become highly specialised, and a patient with several conditions may see many different doctors. Each specialist may prescribe treatments that are sensible in isolation but conflict with one another. Studies of older patients show that taking many drugs at once raises the risk of falls, confusion and hospital admission. Some health systems have introduced coordinated care, in which a single team reviews all of a patient's treatments and agrees priorities with the patient. Early results suggest that such reviews reduce unnecessary prescriptions and improve satisfaction, though savings are hard to prove. Specialists sometimes feel that their expertise is being second-guessed. Patients often report that being asked what matters most to them is new. The challenge is to keep the depth of specialist knowledge while restoring a view of the whole person. Fragmentation is the price of expertise, and coordination is its remedy.
options: Taking many drugs at once lowers the risk of falls and confusion among older patients.
Patients with several conditions benefit most from seeing many specialists, since each prescribes independently.
Coordinated care has proven large savings, so specialists do not need to consider patients' priorities.
Specialised medicine can fragment care so coordinated review focused on patient priorities is being tried.
quests.correctAnswer: Specialised medicine can fragment care so coordinated review focused on patient priorities is being tried.
quests.hint: Choose the option that keeps both the problem of fragmentation and the proposed remedy.
quests.explanation: Specialist care brings depth but also conflicting treatments, and coordination aims to reconcile them, though evidence of savings is limited. The wrong options reverse the benefit of many specialists, overstate savings and reverse the drug risk.
keyPoints: Patients with several conditions may see many specialists whose treatments conflict.
Taking many drugs raises risks for older patients.
Coordinated reviews reduce unnecessary prescriptions and ask what matters to the patient.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Wind farms and solar parks are needed for the shift to clean energy, but they are often opposed by the people who live near them. Objections include changes to the landscape, noise and concern for wildlife. Surveys show that most people in principle support renewable energy, so the gap between general support and local resistance puzzles planners. Researchers find that opposition falls when residents are consulted early, receive a share of the benefits and see that the process is fair. When projects are announced suddenly, or when profits leave the area, resistance hardens even among people who favour renewables. Some communities have proposed alternative sites or designs that reduced the impact. Others have simply opposed everything. Speeding up approvals without earning local consent may achieve short-term gains and long-term backlash. The conflict is less about technology than about trust and fairness.
options: Local resistance to renewable projects reflects perceived fairness more than opposition to clean energy, so early consultation helps.
Speeding up approvals without local consent is the surest way to secure lasting public support.
Resistance falls when projects are announced suddenly and profits leave the area for distant investors.
Most people oppose renewable energy in principle, which explains why local resistance is so strong.
quests.correctAnswer: Local resistance to renewable projects reflects perceived fairness more than opposition to clean energy, so early consultation helps.
quests.hint: Ask why general support and local opposition coexist, and what the last sentence says explains it.
quests.explanation: People broadly favour clean energy but resist unfair or imposed projects, so consultation and benefit-sharing reduce opposition. The wrong options reverse the survey finding, the effect of sudden announcements and the value of speed.
keyPoints: Renewable projects are often opposed by nearby residents despite general support.
Early consultation, shared benefits and fair process reduce opposition.
The conflict is about trust and fairness, not the technology.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Archives cannot keep everything. Governments and organisations produce far more records than any archive can store, so archivists must decide which materials to preserve. This appraisal is a form of judgement about what future generations will want to know. Records of powerful institutions tend to be well preserved, while those of poor or marginal groups may vanish for lack of anyone to keep them. Community archives have emerged to preserve stories that official collections overlook. Digital records add further problems, since file formats become obsolete and storage requires continuing care. Some archivists argue for keeping large samples and cataloguing them lightly, while others prefer selecting a small number of documents and describing them well. Both approaches involve risk, because choices made today shape what history can be written. The shape of the archive is therefore part of the story it tells.
options: Archives keep the records produced by governments, so appraisal is a technical rather than a judgemental task.
Digital records are safer than paper because file formats stay usable and storage needs little care.
Archivists' selections shape which voices survive, so archives partly determine the history that can be written.
Records of marginal groups are usually well preserved, because community archives duplicate official collections.
quests.correctAnswer: Archivists' selections shape which voices survive, so archives partly determine the history that can be written.
quests.hint: See what the final sentence says about the relation between the archive and the story it tells.
quests.explanation: Selection is unavoidable and consequential, so what is preserved influences future historical knowledge. The wrong options deny selection, reverse which records survive and misstate the safety of digital files.
keyPoints: Archives must appraise and select records because they cannot keep everything.
Powerful institutions' records survive more readily, and community archives fill gaps.
Digital formats and sampling choices add risks that shape historical knowledge.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Standard economic accounts count the output of farms, factories and services, but they generally ignore the value of natural systems such as forests, wetlands and fish stocks. A country can therefore appear to be growing while it depletes the resources on which future growth depends. Proposals to include natural capital in national accounts aim to correct this by recording how the stock of nature changes. The task is difficult, since many benefits, such as flood protection or pollination, have no market price and must be estimated. Critics fear that putting a price on nature may encourage the view that anything can be traded for money. Supporters answer that ignoring nature already treats it as worthless. Some governments have begun to publish supplementary accounts alongside the main figures. What is measured tends to be managed, so the choice of what to count is a choice about priorities.
options: Natural-capital accounts would reveal hidden depletion of resources, and valuing nature is difficult and controversial to do.
Standard accounts already record the value of forests, wetlands and fish stocks in national output.
Supporters argue that pricing nature encourages the view that everything can be traded for money.
Governments have replaced their main economic figures with accounts that measure natural capital.
quests.correctAnswer: Natural-capital accounts would reveal hidden depletion of resources, and valuing nature is difficult and controversial to do.
quests.hint: Choose the option that captures both the reason for the proposal and the objection to it.
quests.explanation: Conventional accounts hide depletion, and natural capital accounting aims to show it, but valuation is problematic and disputed. The wrong options reverse existing practice, the supporters' argument and the government response.
keyPoints: Economic accounts ignore natural systems, so depletion can look like growth.
Natural-capital accounting records changes in nature's stock, though many benefits lack prices.
Critics fear commodification, and some governments publish supplementary accounts.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Nutrition advice appears to change constantly, and many people conclude that experts simply cannot agree. Yet most disagreement concerns specific nutrients, such as the effects of certain fats, while broad patterns are more stable. Diets rich in vegetables, whole grains and legumes are linked to better health across many studies, whereas heavily processed foods and sugary drinks are linked to worse outcomes. The difficulty is that diet is hard to study: people misreport what they eat, and trials lasting many years are costly and difficult to enforce. Observational studies can reveal patterns but cannot prove causes. Industry funding of research adds a further reason for caution. Conflicting headlines often arise when a single study is presented as a breakthrough. A sensible reading treats new findings as small adjustments to a stable core rather than as reversals.
options: Observational studies prove the causes of health outcomes, so long trials are unnecessary for nutrition science.
New findings usually reverse earlier advice, so people should treat headlines as breakthroughs.
Experts disagree about broad dietary patterns, though they agree about the effects of specific nutrients.
Dietary advice seems inconsistent because nutrition research is hard, and broad healthy patterns remain stable.
quests.correctAnswer: Dietary advice seems inconsistent because nutrition research is hard, and broad healthy patterns remain stable.
quests.hint: Separate the stable core from the shifting details, then see which option keeps that distinction.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains that apparent contradictions arise from details, methodological limits and media emphasis, while overall patterns stay consistent. The wrong options reverse where disagreement lies, overstate observational studies and misread new findings.
keyPoints: Nutrition advice seems to change, but broad patterns stay stable.
Diet research is hard because of misreporting, costly trials and non-causal observations.
Single-study headlines exaggerate change, so new findings should be treated as small adjustments.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In an economy overflowing with information, human attention has become a scarce resource. Companies compete to capture it, using notifications, autoplay and endless feeds designed to keep people engaged. Behavioural research shows that these features exploit habits that people themselves might not endorse on reflection. Defenders say that users choose freely and get value from the services. Critics answer that choice is limited when systems are built to make stopping difficult. Some countries have begun to regulate certain features for children, and a few platforms have introduced time reminders. It remains unclear whether such tools help, since people often dismiss them. Economists note that the problem is partly one of missing prices: the time people give is not counted as a cost. If attention is a resource, then designing to consume it is a form of extraction that deserves scrutiny.
options: Defenders argue that users cannot choose freely, because systems are built to make stopping difficult.
Attention-capturing design raises questions of consent and cost and defenders and critics disagree about choice.
Reminders have been shown to reduce screen time, so regulation of features is unnecessary.
Economists say that attention is not scarce, since information is overflowing and so is available freely.
quests.correctAnswer: Attention-capturing design raises questions of consent and cost and defenders and critics disagree about choice.
quests.hint: Identify the disagreement between defenders and critics and which point the economists add.
quests.explanation: The paragraph presents attention as a resource captured by design, disputes over voluntariness and the missing-price argument. The wrong options claim proven success, deny scarcity and swap the defenders' and critics' positions.
keyPoints: Human attention is scarce, and firms use features designed to keep people engaged.
Defenders stress free choice, while critics say design limits it.
Reminders and regulation have unclear effects, and attention's cost is not priced.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Laboratories handle hazardous chemicals, radiation and infectious agents, and accidents occasionally happen despite rules and training. Safety researchers find that the safest laboratories are not those with the longest rulebooks but those where people feel able to report near-misses without blame. When errors are punished, staff hide them, and the organisation loses the chance to learn. Some institutions have introduced anonymous reporting and regular discussion of incidents, so that minor problems are corrected before they become serious. Junior researchers, who may be reluctant to challenge senior colleagues, are a special concern, since they often handle the most routine tasks. Leaders influence the culture by how they react when a problem is reported. Some institutions have found that pairing junior and senior researchers on new procedures increases reporting, because juniors gain a trusted person to ask. A safety culture is therefore built on trust, not only on procedure. Written rules matter, but they work only where people are willing to tell the truth.
options: Laboratory safety depends on trust and blame-free reporting of near-misses, not rules alone.
Punishing errors encourages staff to report them, because fear improves attention to hazardous procedures.
The safest laboratories are those with the longest rulebooks, since detailed procedures prevent errors.
Junior researchers are the least likely to be affected by culture, because they follow written rules strictly.
quests.correctAnswer: Laboratory safety depends on trust and blame-free reporting of near-misses, not rules alone.
quests.hint: Decide what the final two sentences say is more fundamental than written procedures.
quests.explanation: Culture and trust enable learning from errors, which rules alone cannot supply. The wrong options reverse the role of rulebooks, punishment and junior researchers.
keyPoints: Laboratories face hazards, and accidents occur despite rules.
Blame-free reporting of near-misses lets organisations learn.
Leaders shape culture, and rules work only where people tell the truth.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Economists have long taught that free trade benefits nations as a whole, since consumers gain from cheaper goods and producers from wider markets. In recent decades, however, research has shown that the gains are unevenly spread. Workers in industries exposed to import competition have lost jobs, and communities that depended on them have struggled for years. The economy as a whole adjusts, but individuals do not move easily to new places or acquire new skills quickly. Policies to help displaced workers, such as retraining and wage insurance, have had mixed success. Some argue that these effects justify limits on trade, while others insist that protection would raise prices for everyone and preserve declining industries. Evidence from several regions shows that the worst-affected communities often lose not only jobs but also local services, which compounds the harm. The dispute has shifted from whether trade creates gains to how those gains should be shared. Aggregate benefits can coexist with concentrated harm.
options: Research shows that free trade harms nations as a whole, though gains are shared equally among workers.
Displaced workers move quickly to new places, so retraining and wage insurance have succeeded.
Free trade brings overall gains and concentrated harm so the debate is now about sharing benefits.
Economists now disagree about whether trade creates gains, rather than about how they should be shared.
quests.correctAnswer: Free trade brings overall gains and concentrated harm so the debate is now about sharing benefits.
quests.hint: See what the final sentences say the dispute is now about.
quests.explanation: Trade produces net benefits, but distribution matters, and policy focus has changed from proving gains to distributing them. The wrong options reverse the aggregate effect, the mobility of workers and the nature of the dispute.
keyPoints: Free trade lowers prices and widens markets, benefiting nations as a whole.
Workers and communities exposed to imports can suffer lasting harm.
The debate has shifted to how gains should be shared and losers supported.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In many countries, occupations from hairdressing to law require a licence. Supporters argue that licensing protects consumers from incompetent or dangerous practitioners. Critics point out that licensing can also limit competition, raising prices and making it hard for newcomers, including migrants, to enter. Studies find that in some trades, licensing raises earnings for practitioners without improving quality noticeably. In others, such as medicine and aviation, the safety benefit is clear. The justification for a licence therefore depends on the size of the harm that unqualified practice could cause and on whether consumers can judge quality for themselves. Some jurisdictions have replaced licences with lighter systems, such as registration or certification, for lower-risk trades. Reforms are often resisted by existing practitioners, who benefit from the barriers that protect their incomes. The aim is to keep protection where it matters and remove barriers where it does not. A licence is a tool, and it suits some tasks better than others.
options: Licensing improves quality noticeably in most trades, so lighter systems would endanger consumers.
Supporters say that licences suit trades where consumers can judge quality for themselves.
Critics argue that licensing lowers prices and makes it easier for migrants to enter occupations.
Licensing protects consumers where risks are serious and restricts competition elsewhere so lighter regimes suit low-risk trades.
quests.correctAnswer: Licensing protects consumers where risks are serious and restricts competition elsewhere so lighter regimes suit low-risk trades.
quests.hint: Consider the criteria the paragraph gives for when a licence is justified.
quests.explanation: Licensing is justified by high risk and consumers' inability to judge quality, and elsewhere lighter approaches reduce barriers. The wrong options overgeneralise the quality effect, reverse the critics' claim and misstate the supporters' criterion.
keyPoints: Many occupations require licences to protect consumers.
Licensing can also raise prices and block newcomers without improving quality.
Justification depends on the risk of harm, so some jurisdictions use lighter regimes.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Sports teams now analyse data on every pass, sprint and shot, and sophisticated models suggest which players to sign and which tactics to use. The results have sometimes been striking: clubs that adopted analytics early found bargains that others overlooked. Yet as more teams use similar methods, the advantage shrinks, because any pattern that is easy to spot is soon copied. Coaches also point out that models struggle with the qualities that matter in a team, such as communication and resilience, which are hard to quantify. Some managers use data as a check on their instincts rather than as a replacement. Fans sometimes complain that a preoccupation with numbers removes the spontaneity of play. Smaller clubs with limited budgets have sometimes gained most, since good information can substitute for expensive players. Data can inform decisions, but it cannot make them. The teams that gain most seem to be those that combine analysis with judgement about people.
options: Managers use data as a replacement for their instincts, since numbers remove the need for personal judgement.
Sports analytics gave early advantages that fade as methods spread, and works best alongside judgement.
Early adopters kept their advantage, because a pattern that is easy to spot is hard to copy.
Sports models capture communication and resilience accurately, so coaches need not rely on judgement.
quests.correctAnswer: Sports analytics gave early advantages that fade as methods spread, and works best alongside judgement.
quests.hint: Note why the advantage disappears and what the last sentence says successful teams do.
quests.explanation: Analytics can find bargains, but widespread use erodes the edge and some qualities resist measurement, so judgement remains essential. The wrong options reverse what models capture, the durability of advantage and managers' use of data.
keyPoints: Teams use data to decide signings and tactics, and early adopters found bargains.
As methods spread, the advantage shrinks, and some team qualities resist quantification.
Teams gain most by combining analysis with judgement about people.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Museums that tell the story of a nation or a people do more than display objects; they help to define what a community remembers. The choice of what is shown, how it is labelled and what is left out shapes visitors' understanding of the past. In recent years, many institutions have tried to include perspectives that were formerly absent, such as those of colonised peoples, women and workers. Some visitors welcome the change, while others feel that the museum has become political. Curators reply that older displays were also selective, though their choices were less visible. Attendance figures do not settle the argument, since visitors may come for different reasons. Some museums now involve communities in planning exhibitions, hoping that shared authorship will make the story more balanced. Exhibition design also matters, since the same object can be framed as trophy, evidence or heritage depending on the text beside it. Memory is not simply preserved but constructed, and museums take part in that construction.
options: Curators argue that older displays were not selective, so newer displays are more political than earlier ones.
Museums preserve the past, so their choices of display and labelling do not affect what visitors understand.
Museums shape collective memory through their choices so including neglected perspectives has prompted debate about neutrality and shared authorship.
Attendance figures settle the argument, showing clearly that visitors prefer displays without neglected perspectives.
quests.correctAnswer: Museums shape collective memory through their choices so including neglected perspectives has prompted debate about neutrality and shared authorship.
quests.hint: Choose the option that captures the last sentence's claim about memory.
quests.explanation: The paragraph argues that museums construct memory through selection, and that inclusion of new voices has stirred debate that co-planning may ease. The wrong options deny museums' influence, reverse curators' claim and misuse attendance.
keyPoints: Museums help define what a community remembers through their displays and omissions.
Many now include perspectives of colonised peoples, women and workers, which some see as political.
Involving communities in planning aims to balance the story.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When workers and employers bargain over pay, the result depends on more than the strength of each side. In countries where wages are negotiated centrally across whole industries, pay differences between workers tend to be smaller, and firms compete on quality rather than on lower wages. Where bargaining is left to individual firms, wages respond more closely to each company's fortunes, and inequality can be greater. Central agreements can be rigid, however, because a single deal may not suit both thriving and struggling firms. Some countries have therefore allowed firms to depart from national terms under specified conditions. Employers often prefer local flexibility, while unions favour broad coverage that prevents undercutting. Studies comparing countries also find that coverage matters as much as the level of bargaining, since exclusions can weaken central agreements. Neither arrangement is superior on every measure. The design of bargaining shapes how the gains and risks of the economy are distributed.
options: Wage bargaining structures trade off inequality against flexibility so many systems mix central and local elements.
One arrangement is superior on most measures, so countries should adopt central bargaining without exception.
Employers prefer national agreements because they prevent undercutting, while unions favour local flexibility.
Central bargaining widens pay differences, so firms compete mainly by cutting wages for their workers.
quests.correctAnswer: Wage bargaining structures trade off inequality against flexibility so many systems mix central and local elements.
quests.hint: Match each bargaining structure with its typical strengths and weaknesses.
quests.explanation: Centralised bargaining compresses pay differences but can be rigid, while local bargaining is flexible but unequal, and some countries blend them. The wrong options reverse the effect of central bargaining, each side's preference and superiority.
keyPoints: Central bargaining tends to reduce pay differences and encourage competition on quality.
Firm-level bargaining is more flexible but can produce more inequality.
Some countries mix the two by allowing departures under conditions.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Commercial aviation has become remarkably safe, and a large part of the credit goes to a culture of learning from failure. Investigators examine every serious accident and publish their findings, which are then used to change procedures and designs worldwide. Crews are encouraged to report errors without fear of punishment, and data from routine flights is analysed to identify risks before they cause harm. This openness is possible partly because the industry shares an interest in safety across competitors. Other fields have tried to copy the approach, with mixed results. In medicine, for example, reporting errors can involve legal risk, and the pressure of time and hierarchy make openness harder. The industry also shares data across national borders, which allows rare events to be studied even when no single airline sees them often. Aviation's success suggests that safety is less a matter of individual vigilance than of systems that turn mistakes into knowledge. The lesson travels only if the conditions that make it work travel too.
options: Investigators keep their findings private to protect airlines, so procedures change within individual companies.
Medicine has copied aviation's approach with success, since reporting errors carries little legal risk.
Aviation became safe because individual pilots are vigilant, so systems for sharing errors matter little.
Aviation's safety comes from systems that turn errors into shared learning, which transfer only under similar conditions.
quests.correctAnswer: Aviation's safety comes from systems that turn errors into shared learning, which transfer only under similar conditions.
quests.hint: Note the final condition on the lesson's transfer to other fields.
quests.explanation: Aviation's approach relies on openness and shared interests, so other fields succeed only if they can create similar conditions. The wrong options reverse the role of individual vigilance, medicine's experience and openness of findings.
keyPoints: Aviation is safe partly because accidents are investigated and lessons shared.
Crews report errors without punishment, and routine data reveals risks.
Other fields have had mixed results, because the conditions matter.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Epidemiological models help governments to decide how to respond to outbreaks, but they can be misunderstood. A model does not predict the future; it shows what might happen under stated assumptions about how people behave and how the disease spreads. Small changes in those assumptions can produce very different curves. During fast-moving outbreaks, data are incomplete and delayed, so early estimates are uncertain and are often revised. The public may interpret revision as failure, and politicians may present a single projection as fact. Officials sometimes feel pressed to announce firm numbers when the honest answer is a range. Modellers increasingly show ranges and scenarios, and they stress that policies themselves change the outcome. Ensembles of models built by different teams can reveal where results agree and where they do not. Good use of a model requires understanding what it can and cannot tell us. It is a tool for reasoning under uncertainty, not a crystal ball.
options: Modellers present single projections as fact, since ranges and scenarios confuse politicians and the public.
Epidemiological models explore scenarios under assumptions, so their uncertainty must be understood rather than treated as prediction.
Epidemiological models predict the future precisely, which is why early estimates are rarely revised.
Small changes in assumptions have little effect on model results, so a single projection can be trusted.
quests.correctAnswer: Epidemiological models explore scenarios under assumptions, so their uncertainty must be understood rather than treated as prediction.
quests.hint: Read the final sentence for how the paragraph characterises a model's proper role.
quests.explanation: Models are conditional explorations, and their usefulness depends on communicating and understanding uncertainty. The wrong options claim exact prediction, deny sensitivity to assumptions and reverse modellers' practice.
keyPoints: Models show what might happen under stated assumptions.
Small changes and incomplete data make early estimates uncertain and subject to revision.
Ranges, scenarios and ensembles help, and models support reasoning under uncertainty.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Effective altruism is a movement that asks how donors can do the most good with limited resources, using evidence to compare charities and causes. Its supporters have directed large sums to interventions, such as distributing bed nets against malaria, that appear to save lives cheaply. Critics say that the approach favours what can be measured, which may overlook long-term, systemic change that resists numbers. They also worry that a focus on the most cost-effective options may discourage support for local causes that people care about. Advocates respond that measuring results is a way of respecting the beneficiaries, not of ignoring them. Some within the movement have extended the logic to distant future risks, which others find speculative. Donors who follow the approach often commit a fixed share of their income, treating giving as a routine rather than an impulse. The debate raises a broader question about whether ethics should be guided by calculation. Numbers can clarify choices, but they cannot decide what deserves our concern.
options: Effective altruism applies evidence to giving, but critics doubt calculation can settle moral priorities.
Effective altruism favours what cannot be measured, because systemic change resists numbers and evidence.
Advocates accept that measuring results ignores beneficiaries, so evidence should play a small role in giving.
The movement supports bed nets and little else, since they save lives at the lowest cost.
quests.correctAnswer: Effective altruism applies evidence to giving, but critics doubt calculation can settle moral priorities.
quests.hint: Watch how the paragraph moves from a method to the deeper question it raises.
quests.explanation: The movement uses evidence to guide giving, while critics doubt that measurement captures everything of value, leading to a question about calculation in ethics. The wrong options reverse the bias, the advocates' response and the scope of the movement.
keyPoints: Effective altruism uses evidence to compare charities, favouring cheap life-saving interventions.
Critics fear bias toward measurable results and neglect of systemic or local causes.
The debate concerns whether calculation should guide ethics.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Police forces increasingly use data to decide where to patrol and whom to watch. Supporters say that analysing past crimes can direct scarce resources to the places where they are most needed. But the data reflect where officers looked in the past, not necessarily where crime occurred. Areas that were heavily patrolled generate more recorded incidents, which can lead to still heavier patrolling, creating a loop that seems to confirm itself. Communities that are already over-policed may feel the effects most. Some departments have audited their systems and limited the kinds of data they use, and others have dropped predictive tools entirely. Researchers suggest that data are more useful for understanding conditions that lead to harm, such as poor lighting, than for pointing at individuals. Civil liberties groups have asked that any predictive tool be open to independent inspection, including its training data and outputs. A tool that learns from unequal records will reproduce their inequality unless someone intervenes.
options: Researchers say data are most useful for pointing at individuals rather than understanding conditions of harm.
Heavily patrolled areas generate fewer recorded incidents, which reduces patrols and breaks the loop.
Police data tools can reproduce past patrols through feedback loops so they need auditing.
Recorded crime reflects where crime occurred, not where officers patrolled, so data tools are neutral.
quests.correctAnswer: Police data tools can reproduce past patrols through feedback loops so they need auditing.
quests.hint: Trace the loop the paragraph describes and decide what the final sentence adds.
quests.explanation: Historic policing shapes the data, which then guides future policing, so unequal patterns persist without intervention. The wrong options reverse the relation between patrolling and records and the researchers' suggestion.
keyPoints: Police forces use data to decide where to patrol and whom to watch.
Data reflect past patrols, creating a self-confirming loop that can burden over-policed communities.
Audits, limits and uses focused on conditions may reduce the harm.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some cities charge drivers to enter their centres, in order to reduce congestion and pollution. After such charges were introduced, traffic fell and public transport use rose. The revenue is used to improve buses and cycling routes, which gives drivers alternatives. Opponents argue that the charge is unfair to those who have little choice but to drive, such as tradespeople or people who live in areas poorly served by transport. Businesses in the centre worry about losing customers, although studies find that trade has generally held up. Public opinion often turns from hostile to supportive after the scheme begins and its benefits become visible. Exemptions and discounts can soften the impact but also complicate the system. Evidence from cities running such schemes for years suggests that traffic reductions persist, although congestion can gradually return as cities grow. Charging works best where good alternatives already exist. The policy changes behaviour by putting a price on what was previously free.
options: Congestion charges cut traffic and fund alternatives and fairness concerns remain.
Charging works best where alternatives are poor, since drivers then have little choice but to pay.
Businesses in city centres lost customers in most cities, so opinion turned strongly against the charges.
Traffic rose after charges were introduced, because drivers who paid felt entitled to use the roads.
quests.correctAnswer: Congestion charges cut traffic and fund alternatives and fairness concerns remain.
quests.hint: Include what the final sentences say about where the policy works best.
quests.explanation: The charge cuts traffic and funds improvements, but fairness objections and the need for alternatives limit its success. The wrong options reverse traffic effects, business results and the role of alternatives.
keyPoints: City centre charges aim to reduce congestion and pollution.
Traffic falls, public transport use rises, and revenue improves alternatives.
Opponents cite fairness, but opinion often becomes supportive once benefits show.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Economists have recently begun to register their study plans in public databases before analysing data, as some other fields do. The aim is to reduce the temptation to try many analyses and report only the ones that produce striking results. Supporters say that registration increases trust in findings. Critics reply that economics often relies on existing data or events that cannot be planned, so a detailed plan may not be possible. Registered studies can also be rigid, leaving little room for unexpected discoveries. Practice has therefore developed in ways that distinguish confirmatory analyses, decided in advance, from exploratory ones that are clearly labelled as such. Journals are experimenting with accepting papers based on their design before the results are known. The change is gradual, and its effect on the credibility of economics remains to be seen. Openness about what was planned helps readers to judge the evidence.
options: Registration is impossible in economics, so exploratory analyses have been banned by journals.
Critics say that registered studies allow unexpected discoveries because plans can be changed freely.
Journals accept papers after the results are known, so design has little effect on publication.
Pre-registration aims to increase credibility and practice separates planned from exploratory analyses.
quests.correctAnswer: Pre-registration aims to increase credibility and practice separates planned from exploratory analyses.
quests.hint: Find how practice is adjusting to the critics' objections.
quests.explanation: Registration seeks to curb selective reporting, and the compromise is to distinguish types of analysis, with credibility effects still uncertain. The wrong options claim registration is impossible, reverse the critics' point about rigidity and misstate journals' practice.
keyPoints: Economists increasingly register study plans before analysing data.
Critics say plans may be impossible or rigid for existing data.
Practice separates confirmatory from exploratory analysis, and journals accept designs before results.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Children who grow up in poverty often start school behind their peers, and the gap can widen over time. Researchers have found that the early years, when the brain develops rapidly, are a critical period for language and social skills. Programmes that support parents, provide high-quality childcare and offer stimulating activities can improve later outcomes. Some long-term studies have followed participants into adulthood and found higher earnings and lower crime. However, results vary, and poorly run programmes have shown little effect. Quality, including well-trained staff and stable relationships, appears to matter more than the label on the programme. Critics add that early intervention cannot compensate for continuing disadvantage at home, such as insecure housing. Programmes that help children while ignoring their families may achieve less than hoped. Cost-benefit analyses often show returns above the initial spending, though benefits arrive decades later. Early support is a strong lever, but it works best as part of wider efforts.
options: Critics claim that early intervention removes the need for addressing housing and other home conditions.
Early childhood support can help disadvantaged children, and quality matters and it cannot offset ongoing disadvantage.
The early years are unimportant for language and social skills, so support can be delayed until school.
Early programmes have consistent benefits in most cases, since quality has little influence on results.
quests.correctAnswer: Early childhood support can help disadvantaged children, and quality matters and it cannot offset ongoing disadvantage.
quests.hint: Note the two qualifications in the final sentences.
quests.explanation: Early support can produce lasting benefits but depends on quality and cannot substitute for improving broader conditions. The wrong options overgeneralise success, deny the early years' importance and reverse the critics' claim.
keyPoints: Children in poverty often start school behind, and the early years are critical.
Quality programmes have shown long-term benefits, while weak ones show little effect.
Early support works best alongside efforts to improve family conditions.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Traditional crafts such as weaving, pottery and woodcarving embody skills passed down through generations. As factories produce similar goods more cheaply, many crafts have lost their markets, and the number of practitioners has fallen. Some governments and organisations have responded by naming master craftspeople and supporting apprenticeships. Others promote craft goods to tourists, though this can push makers to simplify designs for quick sale. Some artisans have adapted, using modern materials or collaborating with designers to reach new customers. Purists worry that such changes dilute the tradition, while others argue that a craft that never changes is a craft that dies. Younger people in craft communities often see better prospects in cities, so the transmission of skills is threatened even when demand for the goods exists. Knowledge held in hands and habits cannot be fully recorded in books or videos. Preserving a craft, then, means sustaining the community of practice, not only the products.
options: Preserving crafts means sustaining communities of practice through apprenticeship and adaptation, not only recording skills.
Tourist demand has encouraged makers to add complexity to designs, which strengthens the tradition.
Purists argue that a craft which changes too much is the one that fades away.
Crafts have kept their markets because factories produce goods that differ greatly from handmade ones.
quests.correctAnswer: Preserving crafts means sustaining communities of practice through apprenticeship and adaptation, not only recording skills.
quests.hint: See what the last sentence says needs to be sustained.
quests.explanation: The paragraph argues that living skills need continued practice among people, and adaptation may be necessary. The wrong options reverse the market situation, the effect of tourist demand and the purists' view.
keyPoints: Traditional crafts embody skills passed down through generations, but many have lost markets.
Support includes apprenticeships and tourism, though adapting can dilute or renew traditions.
Skills cannot be fully recorded, so preserving crafts means sustaining their communities.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Cooperation among unrelated individuals puzzles evolutionary biologists, because helping others is costly while cheating pays. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain how it arises. Repeated interactions allow people to reward helpers and punish cheats, so that reputation matters. Living in small groups makes it easier to identify who has contributed. Cultural norms and institutions can reinforce cooperation by making defection costly. Experiments show that people will pay to punish those who cheat, even when they gain nothing directly. Yet cooperation is fragile, and it can collapse when groups grow large or when trust breaks down. Some scientists emphasise the role of shared identity, which makes people more willing to help those they see as part of the same group. That same loyalty can promote hostility toward outsiders. Field studies in fishing and farming communities show that shared rules can sustain cooperation for generations without any outside enforcer. Cooperation is powerful, but it often comes with boundaries.
options: People refuse to punish cheats when they gain nothing directly, so norms cannot support cooperation.
Shared identity promotes cooperation without hostility toward outsiders, so boundaries do not appear.
Cooperation among unrelated people rests on reputation, norms and shared identity, but it is fragile and bounded.
Cooperation is easy to explain because cheating is costly and helping others pays in evolution.
quests.correctAnswer: Cooperation among unrelated people rests on reputation, norms and shared identity, but it is fragile and bounded.
quests.hint: Watch the closing sentence: cooperation is credited and also qualified.
quests.explanation: The paragraph lists mechanisms for cooperation and then notes fragility and group boundaries. The wrong options reverse the puzzle, the willingness to punish and the effect of shared identity.
keyPoints: Cooperation is puzzling because helping is costly and cheating pays.
Repeated interaction, small groups, norms and punishment help sustain it.
It is fragile, and shared identity can produce hostility to outsiders.
